facts.detail: Ofcom published the Spring 2025 update on 8 May 2025.
The report is a snapshot of fixed and mobile availability as of January 2025.
Gigabit-capable broadband was available to 25.9 million homes, or 86%.
This increased from 25.0 million homes, or 83%, in July 2024.
Gigabit-capable coverage across all residential and business properties was 84%.
Full-fibre service was available to 22.5 million homes, or 74%.
Full-fibre availability increased by 1.8 million homes in six months.
Full-fibre connections reached 9.0 million, up 1.5 million in six months.
Premises without decent fixed or FWA broadband fell to 48,000 from 58,000.
Around 41,000 of those premises were estimated not to be covered by publicly funded rollout in the following twelve months.

guard_streams.source: Superfast Broadband Programme Evaluation: Key Benefits and Impacts
guard_streams.write_limit: Counterfactual programme evaluation findings are historic aggregate evidence and cannot be assigned as current selected-parcel coverage, speed or economic impact.

facts.detail: The key benefits and impacts summary was published on 11 March 2025.
Phase 1 used £530 million of BDUK funding and targeted 90% coverage by December 2016.
Phase 2 added £250 million and targeted 95% coverage by December 2017.
Phase 3 involved more than £1 billion of public funding.
The evaluation estimated a 41 to 47 percentage-point increase in superfast availability in programme areas.
Subsidised coverage was estimated to have created about 23,700 local jobs by the end of 2021.
The whole programme was estimated to increase local business turnover by about £2.6 billion per year by 2021.
Under Phase 3, 292,618 premises had received subsidised coverage by September 2021.
Estimated gigabit additionality peaked at 81% one year after upgrade.
Estimated additionality declined to 49% in the fourth year after installation.

facts.detail: The LFFN Schools interim evaluation was published on 17 October 2022.
Ipsos MORI and George Barrett were commissioned in May 2018.
The project connected 151 primary schools.
The initial target was 104 schools before lower costs allowed expansion.
The installation of fibre was completed by April 2021.
Connected schools were located across 20 local authority areas in England.
About two thirds of the connected schools were in rural areas.
Total funding awarded to school connections was £2.9 million.
The average grant awarded per school was about £19,000.
The evaluation did not identify significant FTTP or ultrafast spillover effects around schools by 2021.

facts.detail: BDUK published the 2021 to 2022 Performance Report on 29 July 2022.
UK gigabit-capable coverage rose from 38.8% to 66.5% during the year.
BDUK subsidies delivered gigabit-capable coverage to 144,000 premises during the year.
The annual minimum target was 120,000 premises.
Cumulative BDUK delivery reached 741,000 premises by March 2022.
The cumulative minimum target was 720,000 premises.
Of the annual delivery, 95,900 premises were previously classed as sub-superfast.
Annual delivery included 95,300 Superfast, 45,000 voucher and more than 3,800 Hub premises or buildings.
BDUK passed 128,300 rural premises, representing up to 89% of subsidised delivery.
Seven initial Project Gigabit procurements were worth over £300 million for up to 200,000 premises.

guard_streams.source: Practical tips for improving your broadband speed
guard_streams.write_limit: Troubleshooting guidance and consumer speed rights do not prove current coverage, orderability or measured speed for a selected parcel.

facts.detail: Ofcom published the broadband-speed tips on 22 December 2023.
The guide was last updated on 24 September 2024.
A provider has one month to improve performance below the promised level before penalty-free exit applies.
Distance from the telephone exchange can affect speed.
Time of day can affect broadband speed.
The number of simultaneous household users can slow a connection.
Ofcom recommends running several speed tests over different days and times.
Electrical devices and wireless equipment can interfere with a router.
A direct Ethernet connection should be faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi.
For telephone-line broadband, Ofcom recommends the main socket, a microfilter and avoiding long extension leads.
